```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A semantic topic is a region of an embedding space: a set of texts whose
vectors lie close to a common center. The region itself has no words, so a
topic has to be described before it can be reported, and the description
is an interpretation that should be traceable to evidence. Two kinds of
evidence are available. The texts nearest the center show what the
members of a topic say. The words that are frequent in a topic and rare in
the others show how it is phrased. The first defines the topic; the
second helps to search and summarize it, and can mislead when it is taken
for the definition.

This guide describes the six topics of the feedback model from both kinds
of evidence, shows which settings change the words and that none of them
changes the topics, and names the topics once they have been read.

```{r setup}
library(sbert)
```

## Data

The model is fitted on the first 600 distinct feedback messages of
`feedback_translations`, with their bundled embeddings, so nothing is
downloaded.

- **`translation`:** the English text of each message; the modeled text.
- **`n`:** the number of times the message occurs in the full corpus.
- **`feedback_embeddings`:** one 384-dimensional `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`
  embedding per message, in the order of `corpus`.

```{r fit}
corpus <- head(dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "translation"), 600)
topic_model <- topics(corpus, n_topics = 6, column = "translation",
                      embeddings = feedback_embeddings)
topic_model
```

The six topics hold 223, 133, 131, 49, 37 and 27 messages. Why six is
discussed in
[Choosing the number of topics and the granularity](choosing-topics.html).

## Which texts show what a topic is?

`representatives()` returns, for every topic, the messages that best
evidence it, ranked in one of two ways.

- `distance` is the cosine distance from a message to the center of its
  own topic: 0 for a message at the center, larger for one at the edge.
  Ranking by distance (`rank = "distance"`) returns the most typical
  messages.
- `margin` is the distance to the nearest other topic minus the distance
  to the message's own topic. A large margin means that the message is
  much closer to its own topic than to any other. Ranking by margin
  (`rank = "margin"`, the default) returns the messages that could belong
  to no other topic.

The text column is long, so the tables are printed with `knitr::kable()`.
The most typical messages first:

```{r reps-distance}
knitr::kable(representatives(topic_model, n = 3, rank = "distance"),
             digits = 2)
```

The most typical messages lie between 0.14 and 0.33 from their centers,
and they make each topic readable: guiding questions followed by an
instruction (topic 1), short hints (topic 2), questions about the meaning
of a phrase (topic 3), corrections (topic 4), explanations of a phrase
mixed with questions about one (topic 5), and descriptions built from
negations (topic 6).

The same topics ranked by margin:

```{r reps-margin}
knitr::kable(representatives(topic_model, n = 3), digits = 2)
```

The two rankings agree where a topic is compact and well separated. For
corrections and negations the margins are 0.40 or more in both tables,
the largest of any topic. They disagree where a topic is diffuse. The most typical
explanations of a phrase (topic 5) have margins of 0.15 to 0.23, because
they also resemble the questions about meaning of topic 3. Ranked by
margin, topic 5 is represented by definitions such as *"Sitting" means
your bottom is on the ground or on a chair*, which lie 0.44 to 0.50 from
the center but cannot be mistaken for a question. Distance shows the
center of a topic; margin shows what separates it from its neighbors.
Reading both is the safer description of a diffuse topic.

## Which words phrase each topic?

`terms()` lists the words that distinguish each topic. By default the
score is class-based TF-IDF (c-TF-IDF; Grootendorst, 2022): the messages
of a topic are treated as one document, and a word scores high when it is
frequent in that document and rare across the others. Each row also gives
the word's `frequency` in the topic and `beta`, its share of the topic's
words.

```{r terms}
terms(topic_model, n = 5)
```

The words describe what the messages are about, not what they do. The
short hints of topic 2 are described, after *ones*, by names of pictures
(*broccoli*, *candy*, *hippo*) that change from message to message. The
negations of topic 6 are described by *person*, *animal* and *hat*, the
objects being ruled out, not by the negation itself. Topics 2 and 3 share
*ones*, although one hints and the other asks.

`terms()` recomputes the words under other settings without refitting
anything. `weighting = "bm25"` replaces the inverse-frequency part of the
score with the BM25 form, which penalizes words shared by many topics more
strongly (Mendonca & Figueira, 2025):

```{r terms-bm25}
terms(topic_model, n = 5, weighting = "bm25")
```

`reduce_frequent_words = TRUE` takes the square root of the within-topic
frequencies before weighting, which keeps a word that a topic repeats many
times from dominating its list:

```{r terms-reduce}
terms(topic_model, n = 3, reduce_frequent_words = TRUE)
```

With either setting the near-ties at the top of topic 1 (*picture*,
*pictures*, *choose*) are reordered, and *choose* now leads topic 1.
`sort_by = "beta"` ranks by the share of the topic instead of by
distinctiveness, which lists the words a topic uses most even when other
topics use them too:

```{r terms-beta}
terms(topic_model, n = 3, sort_by = "beta")
```

## Which words should be left out?

Function words are removed with a stop-word list. `stop_words()` returns
the default English list, and `add` extends it with words that carry no
meaning in a particular corpus. In these messages *ones*, *picture* and
*pictures* occur across the exercises and tell little about a topic:

```{r stop-words}
length(stop_words())
feedback_stop_words <- stop_words(add = c("ones", "picture", "pictures"))
terms(topic_model, n = 3, stop_words = feedback_stop_words)
```

Without them, topic 1 is described by the verbs of its instructions
(*choose*, *pick*, *select*) and topic 2 by its picture names alone.

`stem = TRUE` merges inflected forms under one Porter stem, so *picture*
and *pictures* count as one word. It needs the SnowballC package:

```{r stem, eval = requireNamespace("SnowballC", quietly = TRUE)}
terms(topic_model, n = 3, stem = TRUE)
```

Numbers and Roman numerals are filtered with `numbers = "remove"` and
`roman_numerals = "remove"`, and section numbering with
`section_numbers = "remove"`. The feedback messages contain no digits:

```{r digits}
with(corpus, sum(grepl("[0-9]", translation)))
```

A small example with four invented reports shows the effect. The
embeddings are two-dimensional and made up, and serve only to put the
first two and the last two reports in different topics:

```{r numbers}
reports <- c("Enrolment fell in 2020 and 2021.",
             "Enrolment fell again in 2021, phase II.",
             "Schools reopened in 2022 after closures.",
             "Schools reopened and enrolment rose in 2022, phase III.")
toy_embeddings <- rbind(c(1, 0), c(0.9, 0.1), c(0, 1), c(0.1, 0.9))
toy_model <- topics(reports, n_topics = 2, embeddings = toy_embeddings)
terms(toy_model, n = 4)
terms(toy_model, n = 4, numbers = "remove", roman_numerals = "remove")
```

With the default settings the years lead both topics' lists; removed, the
words that describe the events (*reopened*, *fell*) move up. These filters
apply to the terms only. The text and the embeddings are untouched; to
clean the text itself before encoding, see
[Preparing and cleaning a corpus](preparing-corpus.html).

## Do the term settings change the topics?

They do not. The topics are formed from the embeddings, and the terms are
computed afterwards from the topic assignments and the text. Fitting the
model again with BM25 weighting and the extended stop words, and
cross-tabulating the topic of every message under the two fits, shows the
same partition:

```{r sensitivity}
retuned <- topics(corpus, n_topics = 6, column = "translation",
                  embeddings = feedback_embeddings, weighting = "bm25",
                  stop_words = feedback_stop_words)
assignments <- merge(as.data.frame(topic_model), as.data.frame(retuned),
                     by = "document_id", suffixes = c("_default", "_retuned"))
with(assignments, table(topic_default, topic_retuned))
```

Every message keeps its topic: the table is diagonal, with 223, 133, 131,
49, 37 and 27 messages. The term settings change how a topic is worded,
never which messages it holds, so they can be tuned for readability
without reopening the analysis. Fitting with them, rather than calling
`terms()`, also changes the terms stored in the model, which the plots and
`label = "terms"` use.

## How should the topics be labeled?

By default `topics()` labels each topic with its most central message,
cut at 60 characters. `label = "terms"` labels each topic by its three
top terms instead:

```{r label-terms}
term_labeled <- topics(corpus, n_topics = 6, column = "translation",
                       embeddings = feedback_embeddings, label = "terms")
topic_sizes(term_labeled)
```

Term labels are compact but repeat the weakness of the terms: the labels
of topics 2 and 3 both contain *ones*, and topic 6 is labeled by the objects it
mentions. A message label shows a real member of the topic.

`keywords()` extracts keywords from single documents (the KeyBERT design:
candidate words and phrases are ranked by the cosine similarity of their
embeddings to the document's embedding, then selected by maximal marginal
relevance; Carbonell & Goldstein, 1998). It encodes every candidate, so it
needs a downloaded model and is not run here:

```{r keywords, eval = FALSE}
model_download()
keywords("Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures that are between them.",
         n = 5, ngrams = 2)
```

Once the representatives have been read, `name_topics()` gives the topics
names that state what they are, one per topic in topic order. The names
replace the labels in every table and plot; nothing is refitted.

```{r name-topics}
topic_model <- name_topics(topic_model, c(
  "Guiding question and instruction", "Short hint",
  "Question about meaning", "Correction", "Definition", "Negation"
))
topic_sizes(topic_model)
```

## How coherent are the descriptions?

`summary()` reports the size of every topic and the coherence of its top
ten terms, measured as normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI;
Bouma, 2009): whether the words that describe a topic occur together in
its messages, from -1 to 1.

```{r summary}
summary(topic_model)
```

Coherence is highest for the corrections (0.301), whose messages repeat
*box*, *red* and *blue*, and lowest for the short hints (-0.415), whose
picture names rarely occur together. Low coherence here does not mean a
poor topic: the hints are a clear kind of feedback whose words vary by
design. Coherence evaluates the description, not the topic.
`coherence()` returns the scores as a table. `measure = "umass"` gives
UMass coherence instead (Mimno et al., 2011), a log ratio of co-occurrence
counts that is usually negative and is read the same way, higher being
more coherent:

```{r coherence}
coherence(topic_model, measure = "umass")
```

## How are topics shown in figures?

`type = "terms"` draws the top terms of every topic as bars:

```{r plot-terms, fig.height = 6}
plot(topic_model, type = "terms", n_terms = 6)
```

`type = "representatives"` draws the representative messages, with their
similarity to the center in parentheses:

```{r plot-representatives, fig.height = 6}
plot(topic_model, type = "representatives", n_representatives = 3)
```

`type = "fit"` combines both, one row per topic, and is the figure to
report:

```{r plot-fit, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 9}
plot(topic_model, type = "fit", n_terms = 6, n_representatives = 3)
```

## When to use which

| Question | Verb |
|----------|------|
| What does a topic say? | `representatives(rank = "distance")` |
| What separates it from its neighbors? | `representatives(rank = "margin")` |
| How is it worded? | `terms()`, `terms(weighting = "bm25")`, `terms(sort_by = "beta")` |
| Which words to drop? | `stop_words(add = )`, `numbers = "remove"`, `stem = TRUE` |
| Keywords of one document | `keywords()` (needs a model) |
| Give the topics names | `name_topics()`, or `topics(label = "terms")` |
| How coherent are the words? | `summary()`, `coherence()` |
| Figures | `plot(type = "terms" / "representatives" / "fit")` |
| Every table | `as.data.frame(topic_model, what = "terms" / "representatives")` |

New messages are assigned to the named topics in
[Assigning new documents and topic mixtures](assigning-topics.html), and
the complete analysis of the feedback corpus is in
[Semantic topic modeling with Sentence-BERT](sbert.html).
